```{r options, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6.3, fig.height = 2.5,
  fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H",
  dev = "pdf", cache = FALSE
```

`coo` provides pigeon-inspired colours for categories and continuous
measurements. This short workflow uses R's built-in `mtcars` data to compare
fuel economy and weight, then shows how the same scales work with fills and
direct colour mapping.

## Compare categories

Load the packages and mark the cylinder and gear counts as categories.

```{r setup}
library(coo)
library(ggplot2)
cars <- transform(mtcars, cylinders = factor(cyl), gears = factor(gear))
```

Create a scatterplot and map cylinder classes to the discrete palette.

```{r categorical, fig.cap="Fuel economy and weight, coloured by cylinder class."}
p <- ggplot(cars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  labs(x = "Weight (1,000 lb)", y = "Fuel economy (mpg)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
p + aes(colour = cylinders) + scale_color_coo(name = "Cylinders")
```

The scale selects discrete colours because `cylinders` is a factor. Factors,
character vectors, and logical vectors are categorical; numeric vectors,
including integers, are continuous. For numeric category codes, use a factor
or `scale_color_coo(type = "discrete")`.

Discrete palettes add teal, violet, amber, charcoal, rose, slate blue, then
feather gray. Two categories use teal and violet; six omit feather gray.
The maximum is seven, and requesting more produces an error. For a colour
vector, use `coo_palette(nlevels(cars$cylinders))`.

\newpage

## Show a continuous measurement

Keep the same scatterplot, but colour each car by horsepower.

```{r continuous, fig.cap="The same cars, coloured by horsepower on the continuous ramp."}
p + aes(colour = hp) + scale_color_coo(name = "Horsepower")
```

Numeric data automatically use the continuous ramp from teal through pale
feather gray to violet, interpolated in CIELAB space. It is independent of
the seven discrete colours.
By default, the observed range uses the full ramp, and pale gray marks its
midpoint. Here, the limits are `r min(cars$hp)` and `r max(cars$hp)` hp, so the
centre is `r mean(range(cars$hp))` hp. A constant range maps to pale gray.

For a dark centre, set `mid_color` to wing charcoal. This changes the colour
at the centre; `midpoint` separately controls the numeric value placed there.

```{r charcoal-centre}
charcoal_plot <- p + aes(colour = hp) +
  scale_color_coo(name = "Horsepower", mid_color = "#262D33")
```

To compare plots containing different subsets of cars, reuse the full-data
limits rather than letting each subset choose its own range.

```{r common-limits}
hp_limits <- range(cars$hp)
efficient_cars <- subset(cars, mpg > median(cars$mpg))
efficient_plot <- ggplot(efficient_cars, aes(wt, mpg, colour = hp)) +
  geom_point() + scale_color_coo(limits = hp_limits)
```

For departures from average horsepower, subtract the mean and map zero to
pale gray. Symmetric limits give both halves of the ramp equal space.

```{r centred-values}
hp_difference <- cars$hp - mean(cars$hp)
bound <- max(abs(hp_difference))
centred_colours <- coo_colors(hp_difference, midpoint = 0,
                             limits = c(-bound, bound))
```

An explicit `midpoint` is in original data units and uses
`scales::rescale_mid()`. With asymmetric limits, the nearer endpoint uses only
part of its half of the ramp. Transformations apply before rescaling:
`scale_color_coo(transform = "log10")` has a geometric centre by default.
Use `reverse = TRUE` to swap teal and violet.

\newpage

## Use fills and reuse colour assignments

For filled shapes, use `scale_fill_coo()` with the same discrete/continuous
selection and controls.

```{r filled-bars, fig.cap="Cylinder classes within each gear-count group."}
ggplot(cars, aes(gears, fill = cylinders)) +
  geom_bar() + scale_fill_coo(name = "Cylinders") +
  labs(x = "Gears", y = "Number of cars") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Factor levels control category order. To keep assignments fixed when some
classes are absent, supply the same `limits` or named colours across plots.
The same named mapping can be used outside ggplot2.

```{r stable-categories}
cylinder_colours <- setNames(
  coo_palette(nlevels(cars$cylinders)), levels(cars$cylinders)
)
fixed_scale <- scale_color_coo(values = cylinder_colours)
coo_colors(cars$cylinders[1:6], values = cylinder_colours)
```

`coo_colors()` returns one colour per observation, suitable for a base R
plot's `col` argument. For example, `coo_colors(cars$hp, limits = hp_limits)`
maps horsepower consistently with the continuous example above.

Missing values use `na.value = "grey50"` and do not consume a categorical
colour. Values outside numeric limits are missing by default; use
`oob = scales::squish` to clamp them instead. Both settings work in the scales
and in `coo_colors()`.

Preview all approved palettes with `display_coo()`. For the full argument
reference, see `?scale_color_coo`, `?coo_colors`, and `?coo_palette`.
`scale_colour_coo()` and `coo_colours()` are spelling aliases.
Colour-vision simulations informed the palette, but some pairs remain closer
under red-green deficiencies; pair colours with labels or shapes when needed.
